newsitem.title: GHANA: Rain improves Ghana cocoa prospects - local traders.
newsitem.headline: Rain improves Ghana cocoa prospects - local traders.

text.p: Traders in Kumasi, the centre of Ghana's cocoa industry, say the country has the prospect of a good mid crop and perhaps a bumper main crop if rains continue to be favourable.

"Rains started falling three weeks ago. Now the trees look very healthy with new leaves and sprouts. The rainfall pattern has been favourable. There was enough rain with good strong intermittent sunshine," said one senior trader.

"If the (rainfall/sunshine) pattern continues to be as good as it has been so far, I predict a bumper main crop," added the trader, who heads one of the leading privately-owned cocoa buying companies in Kumasi.

"Yes, there are indications that a bumper (harvest) will come. Usually the light crop determines if the main one will be good. That the rains are drying out (diminishing) now is good for the sprouts on the trees," said a trader of another privately-owned company.
A third trader, from one of the smaller produce-buying companies in Kumasi, was less optimistic, saying he expected "an average kind of output during the mid season".
"Rains have been late in coming. Last year we had them beginning March. This year they came only towards the end of the month (March)," he said.
"Our farmers are also having problems with inputs. There is scarcity of supply of pesticides and insecticides," he added.

All three traders agree that the main crop has been poor in the 1996/97 purchasing year which ended April 3. Previous trade forecasts have put that main crop at between 300,000 and 340,000 tonnes compared with more than 400,000 tonnes in 1995/1996.

"The now closed main crop has been very poor. For cyclical reasons (last year was a bumper crop) and because of the bad rainfall pattern. The rains came at the wrong time, causing black pod," said one trader.
"Black pod used to occur in pockets. Now it is all over the country," he added.
"During the last main season, the chemicals were all the time washed away by the rains that kept falling," explained one of the other traders.
